newsitem.title: FRANCE: Renault stock weak but off lows.
newsitem.headline: Renault stock weak but off lows.

text.p: Shares in carmaker Renault were down on Tuesday but off their lows as investors waited to hear what the company had to say about the proposed Vilvoorde closure at the annual general meeting this afternoon.

The share was down 2.09 percent at 131.20 francs at 1210 GMT but above its low of 129.20 hit after the afternoon newspaper Le Monde reported Renault would appoint an independent expert to explore alternatives to the closure in a political compromise.
"I have no doubt they're going to close the plant," said one Paris-based analyst. "This is nonsense." But other analysts, notably foreigners, said they felt less assured.

"It's highly unclear who is running this company," said a London-based analyst referring to the government, which represents the state's 46 percent stake. "Renault have been passing themselves off as independent... As an investor, I'd feel safer on the sidelines."

The analyst said the decision on Vilvoorde will be key for the markets. "If something as necessary and obvious as the Vilvoorde closure can't be carried out, what chance is there for more radical (corporate) restructuring in France?"
"I think it's foreigners who are selling," one trader said.
But another said foreigners were also buying the share back. Volume was a moderate 281,000 shares.

"The Socialists don't want to ruffle anybody," one stock salesman said. "They want an independent expert to make the decision in order to make it more palatable. That's why the stock isn't falling more. There's not a lot of panic," he said.
Some uncertainty about the timing and cost of the closure had been priced into the stock, brokers said.
Renault has already said the closure date -- initially set for July 31 -- was flexible by weeks or months with the aim of providing the best deal possible for the 2,900 workers left.
But up to now it has not budged on the need to close the plant to streamline its flabby European assembly operations.
"If the conclusion is that the plant stays open, it will be taken extremely negatively (by the market)," said another foreign-based analyst.
One analyst said any move to keep Renault from restructuring would raise serious questions about its long-term prospects. "That could put them potentially on a very dangerous slope."
He said the outcry over Vilvoorde would make it much harder to pursue restructuring moves in France.
The company declined to comment on the report in Le Monde or other media reports about a delay of around six months.
Renault's board is meeting this afternoon ahead of the AGM scheduled to begin at 1500 GMT.
